problem: Recent LVLM-based VLN methods (NaviLLM, NavGPT-2) rely on custom architectures, added modules or simulator-based training, so the potential of plain off-the-shelf LVLMs fine-tuned without architectural changes is unexplored. The effect of low-level vs panoramic action space has also never been tested for LVLMs.
motivation: Modern VLN has moved from egocentric low-level actions to panoramic candidate-viewpoint actions, which assume more prior knowledge (navigable directions) and special panoramic hardware. It is unclear whether generic LVLMs can learn VLN by simple behavior cloning and whether the action-space gap seen for LSTMs persists with LVLMs.
key_idea: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct by behavior cloning on R2R expert trajectories (no architecture change, no simulator in training) with a text prompt that yields either low-level or panoramic candidate actions, and compare the two.
insight: Panoramic beats low-level (41 vs 26 SR test), plausibly because low-level paths have twice as many steps (12.88 vs 6.00 avg) so errors accumulate; offline CSR is 15% vs 3% on val unseen. Plain LVLM fine-tuning remains far below specialized models, likely due to lack of explicit spatial modeling, many visual tokens and BC-only training. In the low-level ablation, removing the auto-turn-to-node step raises SR from 25 to 29, while VFOV 82 vs 105 matters little.
method: Problem formulation: discrete VLN on a navigation graph; at each step the input includes the instruction, observation, history, distance travelled and step number.

Low-level action space: egocentric image plus history of (image, action) pairs; actions Move (to the node closest to view center), Left/Right (30°) and Stop; an automatic 'Turn Towards Node' reorientation is applied before Move and included in history.

Panoramic action space: a 360° panorama (three stitched views) plus separate candidate perspective images, each with relative heading and distance; the model outputs a candidate index or Stop; the panorama and candidates are separate inputs to save memory.
Prompting: fixed system prompt per action space plus a structured multimodal prompt; greedy decoding, no backtracking.

Fine-tuning: behavior cloning with NLL on expert actions, vision encoder and projector frozen and only the LLM tuned; batch size 1, lr 1e-5, 1 epoch over all 3 instructions per path, gradients accumulated per episode.
Evaluation: online in the Matterport3D simulator (SR, SPL, NE, OSR, PL, CLS) and offline (accuracy, macro F1, conservative success rate).

setting.training_data: R2R train split expert trajectories (21,567 instructions total across the dataset; 3 instructions per path, 1 epoch); low-level ablations use only the first 1,955 train trajectories; no extra data
setting.observation: low-level: monocular egocentric RGB (640x480, VFOV 105°, resized to 320x240); panoramic: stitched 360° panorama (960x240) plus candidate perspective images
setting.action_space: low-level: Move / Left 30° / Right 30° / Stop on the nav graph; panoramic: discrete candidate viewpoint index or Stop
setting.simulator: Matterport3D simulator (evaluation and data generation only)
setting.privileged: Navigable candidate viewpoints and their headings/distances from the nav graph (panoramic); allowed-action set U_t (low-level); otherwise none

results: The best model, Qwen2.5-VL-pano, gets 41% SR / 38% SPL on R2R test, beating NavGPT (34% SR) and low-level models (DCF 35% SR, own low-level 26%), but far below NavGPT-2 (72% SR) and NaviLLM (60% SPL). Panoramic beats low-level by 16 SR points on test.
limitations: Behavior cloning only (no student forcing or RL), batch size 1, and a non-standard roughly stitched panorama input, limiting comparability with prior work
Alternative low-level ablations use a small training subset and only the first third of instructions because remote simulator evaluation is slow
Only Qwen2/2.5 small models and English-only R2R were studied; the panoramic action space is not ablated for the effect of panoramic views
